newsitem.title: USA: Dole says he more truthful than "Great Exaggerator".
newsitem.headline: Dole says he more truthful than "Great Exaggerator".

text.p: With Gulf War hero Colin Powell at his side, Bob Dole campaigned in Ohio on Thursday promising voters he would be a more trustworthy president than the "Great Exaggerator" he hopes to oust from the White House in November.

Flanked by Powell and his running mate Jack Kemp, the Republican presidential candidate used a Cincinnati rally to accuse Clinton of overstating his own achievements while distorting Dole's ideas -- themes revisited at sites ranging from a city square to a county fair in an intense day of campaigning by bus in Ohio.
Dole needs to win over swing voters and moderates, but his itinerary took him mostly through solidly Republican parts of the state.
"Now, President Clinton's been talking a lot about a bridge to the future," he told the Cincinnati crowd. "What we really need is a bridge to the truth. A bridge to the truth."
"Remember President Reagan was the great communicator," he said. "President Clinton is the great exaggerator.
"He exaggerates everything that happens in America. He takes credit for everything. If that's the case, he can take the blame for drug use doubling" since he took office, Dole said.

Pitting his "common sense conservatism" against what he called "stealth liberals," Dole attacked Clinton for using scare tactics to disguise a lack of ideas, and of trying to frighten senior citizens, students and veterans by telling them that they would suffer under Dole's tax cuts.
"What ought to scare you is four more years of Clinton and Gore and that's what you ought to be scared of," he said.

"I'm going to tell the truth. And that will be a change too in the United States," he told another rally on a farm in Bloomingburg, where in the shadow of twin silos he reminisced about the days when his father worked in a grain elevator in Kansas.
Dole, Kemp and Powell met in Cincinnati the morning after Kemp's debate with Vice President Al Gore in Florida, which Dole depicted as a Republican victory.

Despite suggestions that Powell, widely seen as Dole's top choice for secretary of state, would be a high-profile campaigner, this was only his second appearance at a campaign event since the Republican convention in August. Dole said Powell added "vim and vinegar and vitality" to the campaign, and would be "one of the stars" of a Dole administration.

Kemp and Powell took part in the opening rally in Cincinnati but did not accompany Dole on the rest of the bus tour, which has Dole crisscrossing urban and rural Ohio for two days in a quest for the state's 21 electoral votes.

Clinton was also in the state on Thursday, campaigning in Dayton. Polls show him ahead in Ohio, as in the nation. In Thursday's tracking poll for Reuters by John Zogby Group International, Clinton led by 8.5 percent, 44.2 percent for Clinton to 35.7 percent for Dole.

"We're solidifying our base everywhere," Dole told reporters outside an ice cream parlour in the small town of Lebanon. "What was it that (Barry) Goldwater used to say -- Go hunt where the ducks are."

The ice cream shop was packed with local Republicans and high school honour students, who watched appreciatively as Dole, a teenage soda jerk back home in Russell, Kansas, joked that the chocolate shakes were as thick as the ones he used to make for himself but not for the customers.
No 20th century Republican has won the presidency without carrying Ohio. The road to the White House goes through Ohio," said Ohio Gov. George Voinovich, introducing Dole at one campaign event.
With the statehouse and most top local offices firmly in Republican hands, Dole should have some help here but polls show he is lagging far behind Clinton, who narrowly carried Ohio in 1992.
